Reference: Salazar Restrepo and Leite Mariante (2026)

Model Setting

The paper asks whether spatially targeted forest conservation survives in general equilibrium, or whether the deforestation it prevents simply relocates, a phenomenon called leakage. It studies two flagship Brazilian policies over 2003-2018: the Priority List (from 2008), which singled out the municipalities with the highest deforestation rates for intensified command-and-control enforcement (embargoes, monitoring priority, credit and registration conditions), and the continuous creation of Protected Areas (Conservation Units and Indigenous Territories), where clearing is banned and which typically cover high-forest, low-deforestation regions. Reduced-form evidence shows both bind locally: a synthetic difference-in-differences design finds that listing cut total natural-vegetation loss by 0.44 log points (36%) while pasture area fell, cropland rose, agricultural value added per hectare rose by roughly 15% and cattle per hectare of pasture by roughly 20%; a spatial regression discontinuity finds forest cover 13-15 percentage points higher just inside Protected Areas. Such designs cannot measure leakage, because they assume untreated regions are unaffected.

The authors build an open-economy quantitative spatial model of Brazil in which deforestation is an economic sector: clearing forest is a costly, decreasing-returns activity that endogenously supplies agricultural land, so each region has an upward-sloping supply curve of new land whose position reflects its deforestation productivity. The economy has 557 micro-regions indexed by rrr (with o,do,do,d for origin and destination) plus a rest of the world (RoW), K=3K=3K=3 agricultural goods (temporary crops, permanent crops, pasture-based cattle) produced with land and labor, and one non-agricultural good. Preferences are non-homothetic (PIGL), workers migrate across regions and select into sectors, goods are traded with iceberg costs, and land accumulates over time. Brazil is modeled as a sequence of static spatial equilibria linked by laws of motion for land and labor. The central theoretical message is that leakage depends on whether targeted deforestation is supply-driven (land is cheap to clear) or demand-driven (land is valuable once cleared), and Brazilian deforestation is predominantly supply-driven.

Household expenditure is local factor income (land rents, labor income and fixed-factor rents) net of deforestation investment, which makes each region's trade balanced in total value (not sector by sector):

Er=vrTrA+yrLLr+(1−γNA)pNArYrNA−prIrD(9.5.6.13)E_r=v_rT^A_r+y^L_rL_r+(1-\gamma^{NA})p^{NAr}Y^{NA}_r-p_rI^D_r \tag{9.5.6.13}Er​=vr​TrA​+yrL​Lr​+(1−γNA)pNArYrNA​−pr​IrD​(9.5.6.13)

where yrLy^L_ryrL​ is average labor income. A competitive equilibrium is a set of prices, wages, land rents, occupational choices, deforestation levels and expenditure shares such that consumers and firms optimize, labor markets clear within the occupational-choice structure, deforestation satisfies the free-entry supply equation, and all goods and land markets clear with trade balance. Between years, land evolves by the accumulation equation and population by migration.

Theory of Leakage

A stripped-down economy organizes the results. Let εD\varepsilon^DεD be the price elasticity of aggregate demand for newly cleared land. In a frictionless benchmark (perfect substitutes across origins, free labor mobility) there is one national price of new land, so deforestation is a pure ZDZ^DZD phenomenon. A ban on a set of regions accounting for share bbb of baseline clearing yields, to first order (Proposition 1),

L=(1−b)εS(1−b)εS+εD(9.5.6.14)\mathcal{L}=\frac{(1-b)\varepsilon^S}{(1-b)\varepsilon^S+\varepsilon^D} \tag{9.5.6.14}L=(1−b)εS+εD(1−b)εS​(9.5.6.14)

Leakage L\mathcal{L}L (increase in non-targeted clearing per unit directly removed) rises with εS\varepsilon^SεS, falls with εD\varepsilon^DεD and falls with bbb. The logic is tax incidence: banning the biggest (cheapest) suppliers leaves a steep residual supply curve, so the induced land-price rise chokes off demand (intensification, substitution toward land-light goods) instead of relocating clearing. Even as b→0b\to0b→0, leakage is capped at εS/(εS+εD)\varepsilon^S/(\varepsilon^S+\varepsilon^D)εS/(εS+εD). Remark 1 explains why leakage grows with the horizon: the relevant demand is for the flow of new land, while farmers demand the stock, so over horizon HHH the flow elasticity is of order εD(H)≈εstock⋅TA/(HTD)\varepsilon^D(H)\approx\varepsilon^{stock}\cdot T^A/(HT^D)εD(H)≈εstock⋅TA/(HTD); in Brazil TA/TD≈53T^A/T^D\approx53TA/TD≈53.

With imperfect substitution across origins (σ>1\sigma>1σ>1), land prices vrv_rvr​ are regional and a region may deforest heavily because clearing is cheap or because land is valuable. For a target (region 1) with deforestation ratio x≡T1D/T2D>1x\equiv T^D_1/T^D_2>1x≡T1D​/T2D​>1, Lemma 1 shows that every relative land price ω≡v1/v2∈[x−1/σ,x1/εS]\omega\equiv v_1/v_2\in[x^{-1/\sigma},x^{1/\varepsilon^S}]ω≡v1​/v2​∈[x−1/σ,x1/εS] corresponds to exactly one pair of relative fundamentals (Z1D/Z2D,Z1A/Z2A)(Z^D_1/Z^D_2,Z^A_1/Z^A_2)(Z1D​/Z2D​,Z1A​/Z2A​); the lower bound is the pure supply-driven economy and the upper bound the pure demand-driven one. For a marginal policy in region 1, Proposition 2 gives

L=1x⋅εS(σ−εD)λ1σ(εS+εD)−εS(σ−εD)λ1(9.5.6.15)\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{x}\cdot\frac{\varepsilon^S(\sigma-\varepsilon^D)\lambda_1}{\sigma(\varepsilon^S+\varepsilon^D)-\varepsilon^S(\sigma-\varepsilon^D)\lambda_1} \tag{9.5.6.15}L=x1​⋅σ(εS+εD)−εS(σ−εD)λ1​εS(σ−εD)λ1​​(9.5.6.15)

where λ1\lambda_1λ1​ is region 1's share of agricultural expenditure, which equals its share of the market value of newly cleared land. Provided σ>εD\sigma>\varepsilon^Dσ>εD, leakage is positive and, holding xxx fixed, strictly increasing in λ1\lambda_1λ1​, hence in the demand-driven share of region 1's deforestation; as σ→∞\sigma\to\inftyσ→∞ it converges to the b→0b\to0b→0 limit of Proposition 1. If instead εD>σ\varepsilon^D>\sigmaεD>σ, conservation in one region would lower clearing everywhere. The authors argue εD<σ=9.6\varepsilon^D<\sigma=9.6εD<σ=9.6 because εD\varepsilon^DεD averages terms (unit factor substitution, θ=2\theta=2θ=2, ζ=6\zeta=6ζ=6) none of which exceeds ζ\zetaζ.

Corollary 1 delivers a sufficient statistic: comparing the target's value share λ1\lambda_1λ1​ with its area share b=T1/(T1+T2)b=T_1/(T_1+T_2)b=T1​/(T1​+T2​),

λ1b=v1vˉ,vˉ≡v1T1+v2T2T1+T2(9.5.6.16)\frac{\lambda_1}{b}=\frac{v_1}{\bar{v}},\qquad \bar{v}\equiv\frac{v_1T_1+v_2T_2}{T_1+T_2} \tag{9.5.6.16}bλ1​​=vˉv1​​,vˉ≡T1​+T2​v1​T1​+v2​T2​​(9.5.6.16)

A ratio below one (many hectares, little value) signals supply-driven, low-leakage targeting; a ratio above one signals demand-driven, high-leakage targeting. In raw data (2003-2007 clearing weighted by 2006 census land values), the regions that would enter the Priority List account for 36% of cleared area but under 20% of its value, a ratio of 0.55; a same-size set of the highest-land-value regions has 10% of value on 1.6% of area, a ratio of 6.3.

Calibration and Model Inversion

Structural parameters are estimated outside the equilibrium solution. The load-bearing parameter is δ\deltaδ, estimated from the supply equation on municipality-year data, 2008-2018:

Because rents are endogenous, log⁡vrt\log v_{rt}logvrt​ is instrumented with a shift-share (Bartik) index: world commodity prices interacted with each municipality's base-year crop mix. For all Brazil the IV elasticity is 0.68 (s.e. 0.28), implying δ≈0.41\delta\approx0.41δ≈0.41 and εS≈0.70\varepsilon^S\approx0.70εS≈0.70; on the Legal-Amazon frontier it is 1.66 (s.e. 0.43), implying δ≈0.62\delta\approx0.62δ≈0.62 and εS≈1.63\varepsilon^S\approx1.63εS≈1.63. The baseline uses δ=0.41\delta=0.41δ=0.41 because the model covers all of Brazil and generates regional differences in the land margin through forest availability. Other values: ψ=0.26\psi=0.26ψ=0.26 (from micro-regions plausibly at their forest steady state), ρ=0.01\rho=0.01ρ=0.01 (observed regrowth), αk=(0.74;0.47;0.85)\alpha_k=(0.74;0.47;0.85)αk​=(0.74;0.47;0.85) for temporary crops, permanent crops and pasture (2006 census), γNA=0.66\gamma^{NA}=0.66γNA=0.66, (χA,χNA,ι)=(1.55;1.52;12.8)(\chi^A,\chi^{NA},\iota)=(1.55;1.52;12.8)(χA,χNA,ι)=(1.55;1.52;12.8) from Alvarez (2020), ϕ=0.01\phi=0.01ϕ=0.01 and ν=0.12\nu=0.12ν=0.12 from Eckert and Peters (2022), η=0.506\eta=0.506η=0.506 (2017/18 expenditure survey), σ=9.6\sigma=9.6σ=9.6 and ζ=6\zeta=6ζ=6 from Dominguez-Iino (2026), θ=2\theta=2θ=2, ϵ=1.22\epsilon=1.22ϵ=1.22 and μdo\mu^o_dμdo​ from 2010-census migration gravity, κ=0.105\kappa=0.105κ=0.105 from interstate trade gravity, and β=0.95\beta=0.95β=0.95.

Identification and the Content of ZDZ^DZD

With inverted fundamentals, PPML regressions of observed deforestation (year and micro-region fixed effects) show that the supply side alone (ZˉD\bar{Z}^DZˉD and natural area) reaches a pseudo-R2R^2R2 of 0.955, against 0.853 for all demand-side fundamentals including market access. In the full specification the coefficient on ln⁡ZˉrD\ln\bar{Z}^D_rlnZˉrD​ is 1.67, almost exactly the model-implied 1/(1−δ)=1.691/(1-\delta)=1.691/(1−δ)=1.69. To show that ZDZ^DZD is not a fudge factor, the authors regress it on variables external to the inversion: hot, dry clearing seasons raise it, carbon density lowers it, and climate and biomass explain about a third of its cross-regional variation (about 40% with enforcement); lagged IBAMA fines per unit deforested are negatively related to it within regions. The inverted model also reproduces the Priority List's value-to-area ratio (0.58 against the raw 0.55) without targeting it.

Conservation Policies in the Model

Policies enter as shifts in deforestation productivity. For the Priority List, a micro-region is listed if any of its municipalities is (69 municipalities in 31 of the 557 micro-regions). A PPML regression of the inverted base productivity on listing with region and year fixed effects estimates the policy shock, which is then removed to build the no-policy productivity, with forest stocks re-simulated in all regions:

E(ZˉrtD∣r,t,Priorityrt)=exp⁡(αr1+αt2+βPLPriorityrt),(ZrtD)nopolicy=ZˉrtDexp⁡(β^PL)((TrtF)nopolicy)ψ(9.5.6.19)E\left(\bar{Z}^D_{rt}\mid r,t,\text{Priority}_{rt}\right)=\exp\left(\alpha^1_r+\alpha^2_t+\beta^{PL}\text{Priority}_{rt}\right),\qquad (Z^D_{rt})^{nopolicy}=\frac{\bar{Z}^D_{rt}}{\exp(\hat{\beta}^{PL})}\left((T^F_{rt})^{nopolicy}\right)^{\psi} \tag{9.5.6.19}E(ZˉrtD​∣r,t,Priorityrt​)=exp(αr1​+αt2​+βPLPriorityrt​),(ZrtD​)nopolicy=exp(β^​PL)ZˉrtD​​((TrtF​)nopolicy)ψ(9.5.6.19)

For Protected Areas, the base productivity is unchanged but the convertible forest shrinks; assuming perfect enforcement, the no-policy world adds back the area TrtPT^P_{rt}TrtP​ protected since 2003:

(ZrtD)nopolicy=ZˉrtD((TrtF)nopolicy+TrtP)ψ(9.5.6.20)(Z^D_{rt})^{nopolicy}=\bar{Z}^D_{rt}\left((T^F_{rt})^{nopolicy}+T^P_{rt}\right)^{\psi} \tag{9.5.6.20}(ZrtD​)nopolicy=ZˉrtD​((TrtF​)nopolicy+TrtP​)ψ(9.5.6.20)

The Priority List is a partial ban: at fixed prices it cuts listed regions' supply of new land by the fraction f=1−exp⁡(β^PL)1/(1−δ)=0.48f=1-\exp(\hat{\beta}^{PL})^{1/(1-\delta)}=0.48f=1−exp(β^​PL)1/(1−δ)=0.48, so with listed regions accounting for b=0.37b=0.37b=0.37 of pre-policy national deforestation, it removes bf=0.18bf=0.18bf=0.18 of national new-land supply. The fixed-price cut (48%) exceeds the reduced-form equilibrium reduction (36%), consistent with general-equilibrium dampening inside listed municipalities.

Measuring Leakage

Counterfactual A (no policy) simulates 2003-2018 with (ZrtD)nopolicy(Z^D_{rt})^{nopolicy}(ZrtD​)nopolicy, solving the full equilibrium each year. Counterfactual B (policy, no leakage) is an accounting device: it combines the with-policy productivities with the no-policy prices, shutting down every price channel (labor and goods markets) through which clearing could relocate:

(TrD)noleakage=(δ(qr)nopolicy(pr)nopolicy)δ1−δ(ZrD)11−δ(9.5.6.21)(T^D_r)^{noleakage}=\left(\delta\frac{(q_r)^{nopolicy}}{(p_r)^{nopolicy}}\right)^{\frac{\delta}{1-\delta}}\left(Z^D_r\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\delta}} \tag{9.5.6.21}(TrD​)noleakage=(δ(pr​)nopolicy(qr​)nopolicy​)1−δδ​(ZrD​)1−δ1​(9.5.6.21)

The gap between A and B is the gross avoided deforestation (fixed-price direct effect); the gap between the data and B is the general-equilibrium effect. Leakage at horizon ttt is the share of avoided deforestation undone by general-equilibrium adjustment:

Leakaget=∑r[(TrtD)policy−(TrtD)noleakage]∑r[(TrtD)nopolicy−(TrtD)noleakage](9.5.6.22)\text{Leakage}_t=\frac{\sum_r\left[(T^D_{rt})^{policy}-(T^D_{rt})^{noleakage}\right]}{\sum_r\left[(T^D_{rt})^{nopolicy}-(T^D_{rt})^{noleakage}\right]} \tag{9.5.6.22}Leakaget​=∑r​[(TrtD​)nopolicy−(TrtD​)noleakage]∑r​[(TrtD​)policy−(TrtD​)noleakage]​(9.5.6.22)

This is a Laspeyres-type decomposition (the direct effect is priced at no-policy prices) and counts price-driven clearing wherever it lands, including inside the targeted regions. Areas are converted to carbon using region-specific carbon densities of natural ecosystems.

Key Results

  • Leakage is small. Over 2003-2018 the Priority List avoided 80,051 km2^22 gross, with 2,935 km2^22 leaking back: 77,116 km2^22 net and leakage of 3.7%. Protected Areas avoided 7,311 km2^22 gross, 467 km2^22 leaked, 6,844 km2^22 net, leakage 6.4%. Net avoided emissions are 4.1 and 0.34 Gt of CO2_22​; carbon leakage is 3.0% and 5.5%, lower because targeted regions are carbon-dense.

  • Range. Re-solving at the frontier δ=0.62\delta=0.62δ=0.62, leakage rises to 8.8% (Priority List) and 14.7% (Protected Areas), so the policies retain at least about 91% and 85% of their gains. Only far above the identified range does leakage grow (about 12% and 20% at δ=0.70\delta=0.70δ=0.70; 20% and 32% at δ=0.80\delta=0.80δ=0.80).

  • Geography. About 60% of the Priority List's general-equilibrium effect occurs inside listed regions (in-situ price responses); relocation to untargeted regions is about 1.5% of avoided deforestation, some 1,200 km2^22. Absorption is concentrated (the top decile of the 526 untargeted regions takes 45%) and is predicted by the receivers' ZrDZ^D_rZrD​ with an elasticity near one, while market access enters negatively: displaced clearing flows to the next-cheapest, remote clearers.

  • Targeting. Holding scope fixed, the actual Priority List and a highest-deforestation rule both leak 3.7%, a highest-ZDZ^DZD rule leaks 3.3%, and a highest-land-value (demand-driven) rule leaks 36% while avoiding almost nothing (732 km2^22 net, against 79,635 for the actual policy in the same exercise); the value-to-area ratio of that rule is 11.

  • Horizon. Leakage is a path: 0.7% in the first policy year rising to 3.7% by 2018, as predicted by the stock-flow logic of Remark 1.

Extensions

Open versus closed economy: switching off RoW gives 3.2% (Priority List) and 5.7% (Protected Areas), because world demand both raises εD\varepsilon^DεD and makes demand for Brazilian land less satiable, and these nearly cancel. Parameter sweep: 54 of 55 single-deviation re-inversions converge; apart from δ\deltaδ, no parameter moves Priority List leakage by more than 0.6 percentage points (largest mover α\alphaα), shutting internal migration leaves it at 3.7% (workers switch sectors locally instead), and the Priority List leaks less than Protected Areas in every converged cell. Swap counterfactual: reassigning all variation to the demand side cannot reproduce Brazil's deforestation dispersion. SUTVA bias: running the synthetic difference-in-differences estimator on model-generated panels, spillovers attenuate the estimate by 0.013 log points (about 3%), and the model analogue (−0.43-0.43−0.43) matches the actual estimate (−0.44-0.44−0.44). Structural transformation and welfare: by 2018 the Priority List raises the national agricultural employment share by 0.10 percentage points (about 96,000 workers) through intensification and leaves real income per worker essentially unchanged; the implied general-equilibrium cost is about −0.001-0.001−0.001 dollars per tonne of CO2_22​ (Priority List) and −0.004-0.004−0.004 (Protected Areas), far below social costs of carbon of roughly 50 to 190 dollars, though this excludes fiscal enforcement costs and masks distributional incidence.

This is the law of motion that links the yearly static equilibria. TrtAT^A_{rt}TrtA​ is the stock of agricultural land in region rrr at the start of year ttt (hectares), TrtDT^D_{rt}TrtD​ is the flow of newly cleared land during year ttt, and ρ\rhoρ is the constant fraction of agricultural land that reverts to natural vegetation each year (calibrated to ρ=0.01\rho=0.01ρ=0.01). Land therefore behaves like a capital stock: regrowth plays the role of depreciation and deforestation the role of gross investment. Land cleared in year ttt becomes productive in year t+1t+1t+1.

Two implications are used later. First, if deforestation settles at a constant flow, the stock converges to the steady state

TrA∗=TrDρT^{A*}_r=\frac{T^D_r}{\rho}TrA∗​=ρTrD​​

so regrowth is what allows a positive long-run deforestation flow with a finite land stock. Second, the stock is large relative to the flow (in Brazil TA/TD≈53T^A/T^D\approx53TA/TD≈53), so a given percentage change in the desired stock of land translates into a much larger percentage change in the demanded flow of new land. This stock-flow logic is behind the horizon dependence of leakage discussed after equation (14): the flow demand elasticity is huge in the short run and falls as the horizon lengthens. The survival factor 1−ρ1-\rho1−ρ also enters the capitalization of rents into land prices in equation (6), and the same law of motion is applied in the no-policy counterfactual with (TrtD)nopolicy(T^D_{rt})^{nopolicy}(TrtD​)nopolicy.

This is the assumed technology of the deforestation sector. IrDI^D_rIrD​ is the quantity of the local final good (the same Cobb-Douglas bundle that households consume, priced at prp_rpr​) spent on clearing, TrDT^D_rTrD​ is the area of new agricultural land produced, and ZrDZ^D_rZrD​ is deforestation productivity, the number of hectares obtained from one unit of the final good at IrD=1I^D_r=1IrD​=1. The parameter δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1)δ∈(0,1) is the output elasticity of clearing effort; because δ<1\delta<1δ<1 there are decreasing returns within the year, interpreted as forest near the edge being cheaper to clear than forest deeper inside.

Inverting the technology gives the cost of clearing TTT hectares,

which is convex, so marginal cost rises with the area cleared and each region has an upward-sloping supply curve of new land. This is what the functional form buys: a constant supply elasticity δ/(1−δ)\delta/(1-\delta)δ/(1−δ), derived in equation (3), and a clean log-additive separation between ZrDZ^D_rZrD​ and prices. It rules out constant returns (δ=1\delta=1δ=1), under which supply would be infinitely elastic and any local conservation policy would leak almost completely, and it rules out a supply elasticity that varies with the level of clearing, apart from the depletion effect that enters through ZrDZ^D_rZrD​ in equation (4). The parameter δ\deltaδ is estimated from equation (17).

This equation makes deforestation productivity depend on how much forest is left. TrFT^F_rTrF​ is the area of unprotected natural vegetation in region rrr that can still be converted, ZˉrD\bar{Z}^D_rZˉrD​ is the base (forest-invariant) productivity, and ψ>0\psi>0ψ>0 is the elasticity of productivity with respect to available forest, calibrated to ψ=0.26\psi=0.26ψ=0.26. The log-log form is motivated empirically: forest area is a strong predictor of the inverted ZrDZ^D_rZrD​ and a log-log relationship fits well.

The form buys three things. First, a depletion channel: as a region clears its forest, TrFT^F_rTrF​ falls, ZrDZ^D_rZrD​ falls, and its supply curve of new land shifts in, so deforestation reaches a steady state instead of exhausting the forest in finite time. Combining with equation (3), the fixed-price elasticity of deforestation with respect to remaining forest is

∂ln⁡TrD∗∂ln⁡TrF=ψ1−δ≈0.44at δ=0.41\frac{\partial\ln T^{D*}_r}{\partial\ln T^F_r}=\frac{\psi}{1-\delta}\approx 0.44\quad\text{at }\delta=0.41∂lnTrF​∂lnTrD∗​​=1−δψ​≈0.44at δ=0.41

Second, it gives regional heterogeneity in the land margin even with a common δ\deltaδ, which is the argument for the all-Brazil baseline value of δ\deltaδ. Third, it gives each policy a clean entry point: the Priority List shifts ZˉrD\bar{Z}^D_rZˉrD​ (equation (19)), while Protected Areas shrink TrFT^F_rTrF​ (equation (20)). The base term ZˉrD\bar{Z}^D_rZˉrD​ is a residual that bundles terrain, climate, enforcement, timber revenue and titling expectations, that is, every determinant of clearing that is not a demand-side fundamental.

These constant shares are what Cobb-Douglas buys: land rents and labor income can be read directly from observed revenues (equations (12) and (18)) before any price or productivity is known. It imposes a unit elasticity of substitution between land and labor, so a higher land rent induces intensification (more labor per hectare) one for one; this unit elasticity is one of the components of the demand elasticity for new land εD\varepsilon^DεD in equations (14) and (15). Pasture has the highest land share, so cattle is the most land-intensive activity and the one most affected when land becomes scarce. Because HrH_rHr​ is fixed, the non-agricultural sector has decreasing returns to labor, which limits how much labor it can absorb at a given wage; its rents, a share 1−γNA1-\gamma^{NA}1−γNA of non-agricultural value added, go to local residents and enter equation (13).

Two remarks. First, the formula counts the first rent in the current period (s=0s=0s=0). If instead the first rent arrived one period after clearing, as the timing of equation (1) suggests, the price would carry an extra factor β\betaβ; this is a constant that is absorbed into the level of the inverted ZrDZ^D_rZrD​ and does not affect elasticities or counterfactual changes. This is the assumed indirect utility function, of the price-independent generalized linear (PIGL) class. eee is the household's nominal expenditure, pAp^ApA and pNAp^{NA}pNA are the price indices of the agricultural and non-agricultural composites, and (pA)ϕ(pNA)1−ϕ(p^A)^{\phi}(p^{NA})^{1-\phi}(pA)ϕ(pNA)1−ϕ is a Cobb-Douglas price index, so the first term is a power function of real expenditure. The parameter η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1)η∈(0,1) governs how fast the composition of spending changes with income (the Engel elasticity, 0.5060.5060.506), ϕ\phiϕ is the asymptotic agricultural share of very rich households (0.010.010.01), and ν>0\nu>0ν>0 scales the non-homothetic component (0.120.120.12). The second term lowers utility when food is relatively expensive, over and above the effect through the price index, and it does so by the same amount for rich and poor; relative to the first term it matters more for the poor, which is how the function encodes that food is a necessity.

The form is chosen because it delivers a closed-form expenditure share that falls with income, derived in equation (10), while still aggregating: the regional share depends only on mean expenditure and one statistic of dispersion. Setting ν=0\nu=0ν=0 gives homothetic Cobb-Douglas preferences with constant share ϕ\phiϕ. OLS is inconsistent because rents are an equilibrium outcome: a positive supply shock expands the land stock and lowers rents, and reverse causality biases the coefficient. The shift-share instrument interacts world commodity prices (shifts) with each municipality's base-year crop mix (shares), which moves the demand for land and traces out the supply curve. Identification requires that world price movements, weighted by predetermined crop exposure, are unrelated to local changes in clearing costs. The first part is a regression that measures how much the Priority List lowered deforestation productivity; the second builds the counterfactual productivity without the policy. ZˉrtD\bar{Z}^D_{rt}ZˉrtD​ is the base productivity recovered from the inversion (equation (4)), Priorityrt\text{Priority}_{rt}Priorityrt​ equals one if micro-region rrr is listed in year ttt, αr1\alpha^1_rαr1​ and αt2\alpha^2_tαt2​ are region and year fixed effects, and βPL\beta^{PL}βPL is the proportional shift in base productivity caused by listing. The exponential mean is estimated by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood, which suits a positive, multiplicative, heteroskedastic outcome and avoids the retransformation bias of a log-linear regression. Identification is difference-in-differences: βPL\beta^{PL}βPL comes from within-region changes in ZˉrtD\bar{Z}^D_{rt}ZˉrtD​ around listing relative to unlisted regions in the same year, under the assumption that base productivity would otherwise have evolved in parallel. Using ZˉrtD\bar{Z}^D_{rt}ZˉrtD​ instead of observed deforestation as the outcome means that equilibrium price responses have already been stripped out by the inversion.

The counterfactual divides the base productivity of listed region-years by exp⁡(β^PL)\exp(\hat{\beta}^{PL})exp(β^​PL); for unlisted region-years the divisor is one, so the general expression is ZˉrtD/exp⁡(β^PLPriorityrt)\bar{Z}^D_{rt}/\exp(\hat{\beta}^{PL}\text{Priority}_{rt})ZˉrtD​/exp(β^​PLPriorityrt​), a qualification that the equation in the note leaves implicit. This equation builds the no-policy deforestation productivity for the Protected Areas counterfactual. Undoing the policy means adding the protected area back to the forest available for clearing.

The construction rests on perfect enforcement: clearing inside Protected Areas is taken to be zero, so protected forest is simply absent from TrtFT^F_{rt}TrtF​ in the observed economy. It also explains why Protected Areas leak more: they remove supply from regions that are not the cheapest clearers, leaving elastic supply elsewhere.

In untargeted regions whose productivity is unchanged the direct effect is one and any difference from the no-policy path is a price effect. In a listed region the direct effect is 1−f1-f1−f from equation (19), and a price effect above one means that some of the avoided clearing returns inside the targeted region itself. Counterfactual B is not an equilibrium, since markets do not clear at these quantities; it is an accounting device.

This is the definition of leakage used in the quantitative results. For each region rrr and year ttt there are three deforestation levels: (TrtD)policy(T^D_{rt})^{policy}(TrtD​)policy, the observed data, which the inverted model matches exactly; (TrtD)nopolicy(T^D_{rt})^{nopolicy}(TrtD​)nopolicy, counterfactual A; and (TrtD)noleakage(T^D_{rt})^{noleakage}(TrtD​)noleakage, counterfactual B from equation (21). The denominator is gross avoided deforestation, the fixed-price direct effect of the policy. The numerator is the general-equilibrium effect, the clearing induced by price changes. The total effect of the policy decomposes exactly:

∑r[(TrtD)nopolicy−(TrtD)policy]⏟net avoided=∑r[(TrtD)nopolicy−(TrtD)noleakage]⏟gross avoided−∑r[(TrtD)policy−(TrtD)noleakage]⏟leaked\underbrace{\sum_r\left[(T^D_{rt})^{nopolicy}-(T^D_{rt})^{policy}\right]}_{\text{net avoided}} =\underbrace{\sum_r\left[(T^D_{rt})^{nopolicy}-(T^D_{rt})^{noleakage}\right]}_{\text{gross avoided}} -\underbrace{\sum_r\left[(T^D_{rt})^{policy}-(T^D_{rt})^{noleakage}\right]}_{\text{leaked}}net avoidedr∑​[(TrtD​)nopolicy−(TrtD​)policy]​​=gross avoidedr∑​[(TrtD​)nopolicy−(TrtD​)noleakage]​​−leakedr∑​[(TrtD​)policy−(TrtD​)noleakage]​​

so net avoided deforestation equals gross avoided deforestation times 1−Leakaget1-\text{Leakage}_t1−Leakaget​. A value of zero means that prices undo nothing; a value of one means that the policy has no aggregate effect. For the Priority List, 2,935/80,051≈0.0372{,}935/80{,}051\approx0.0372,935/80,051≈0.037; for Protected Areas, 467/7,311≈0.064467/7{,}311\approx0.064467/7,311≈0.064.

Three features of the definition matter. The sums run over all regions, so price-driven clearing is counted wherever it occurs, including inside targeted regions; this is broader than the theoretical L\mathcal{L}L of equations (14) and (15), which counts only clearing in untargeted regions. The direct effect is valued at no-policy prices, a Laspeyres convention; valuing it at with-policy prices would move mass between the two pieces without changing the net effect. And the statistic is reported cumulatively over the horizon up to ttt, which is why it rises over time as the land stock adjusts through equation (1). Replacing areas by carbon contents gives carbon leakage.
